_note: Ranking the World's Most Polite Languages, recounted 2026-10-24 with the expanded database in polite_research/ (English Wiktionary for ~100 languages, 16 native Wiktionaries, JMdict, CC-CEDICT, Poedjosoedarmo's Javanese word list; one rule set, duplicates and expressions removed, see polite_research/README.md). Tibetan (52, would be #9) has no recording of a polite word on Commons, so it is skipped. Vietnamese (83) counted after fixing syllable spacing.
title: Ranking the World's Most Polite Languages
subtitle: BY THE NUMBER OF POLITE WORDS IN THE DICTIONARIES
outro: Which language is the most polite?

items.name: Chinese
cards: To ask a stranger's name politely you don't say 'what's your name?' but 'your precious surname?' (贵姓). Even 'you' has a polite form: 您 (nín).
The humble side counts too: traditionally your own home is 'my cold hut' (寒舍) and your own work 'my clumsy work' (拙作).

items.name: Japanese
cards: Japanese politeness has three layers: polite words, honorific words that raise others, and humble words that lower yourself.
Even 'to be' changes: iru with friends, irassharu for someone you respect, and oru for yourself when being humble.

items.name: Javanese
items.lit: to eat (said of someone you honour)
cards: Javanese has separate vocabularies by social level: ngoko for friends, krama for elders and strangers, krama inggil for the deepest respect.
Even 'eat' changes: mangan with friends, nedha in polite speech, and dhahar for someone you honour. A scholarly list counts over 900 of these polite words.

items.name: Korean
cards: Korean grammar has up to seven speech levels, built into the end of every verb.
Even eating changes: 먹다 (meokda) for yourself, 잡수시다 (japsusida) for your elders. That politeness lives in grammar too, so a word count underrates Korean.

items.name: Thai
items.word: สวัสดีครับ
items.lit: hello + the polite 'khrap' (said by a man)
cards: Thai ends polite sentences with a little word that depends on who is talking: 'khrap' if you are a man, 'kha' if you are a woman.
Thai has a whole royal vocabulary, rachasap: special words used only for the king and the royal family. Most of its count comes from them.

items.name: Burmese
cards: Burmese has no surnames, so a title carries the respect: U for an older man, Daw for an older woman, Ko for a young man, Ma for a young woman.
Polite sentences end with a softening 'pa', and men add 'khinbya' (ခင်ဗျာ) at the end to sound extra respectful.

items.name: Vietnamese
cards: Vietnamese has no neutral 'I' or 'you': speakers pick family words like older brother, aunt or grandfather, depending on age and respect.
Answering an elder with a bare 'yes' sounds rude. Children learn to say 'dạ', and to end their sentences with 'ạ' to show respect.

items.name: English
cards: English lost its polite 'you'. 'Thou' was the friendly one and 'you' the polite one, until everyone became 'you'.
In Britain 'cheers' isn't just for drinks: it means thank you, and even goodbye. English is polite with phrases more than special words.

items.name: Indonesian
cards: Indonesian has a polite 'he/she': beliau, used for teachers, elders and leaders, instead of the everyday 'dia'.
Indonesians use family titles with everyone: Bapak (father) for any older man, Ibu (mother) for any older woman, even in shops and offices.

items.name: Malay
items.lit: I (humbly, when speaking to a king)
cards: Malay has a royal vocabulary too: a king does not eat (makan) but 'santap', does not sleep (tidur) but 'beradu', and does not die (mati) but 'mangkat'.
Speaking to a sultan you don't call yourself 'saya' but 'patik', and you call him 'tuanku', my lord.
